profile.reading:
Per Vantage Data Centers' own facility page, this building, VA2, sits on the Ashburn II campus at 22435 Glenn Drive, Sterling, VA 20164. Vantage describes the 18-acre campus as three multi-story facilities totaling 800,000 square feet and 96 megawatts of critical IT load, built to N+1 power and N+2 mechanical redundancy with six main meet-me rooms and three points of entry; the operator states a sustainability goal of net-zero carbon emissions campus-wide by 2030. No individual per-building sqft or MW breakdown is published for the three Ashburn II buildings, and no formal third-party certification (LEED, Uptime Tier) is listed on this page.

Vantage is a private, Denver, Colorado-headquartered operator; DigitalBridge acquired the company in March 2017, and in January 2024 Vantage announced a $6.4 billion equity investment round led by DigitalBridge and Silver Lake, with Colony Capital, AustralianSuper, GIC, and ADIA cited among its other investors. Virginia's data center boom is reshaping statewide electricity rates directly relevant to every Ashburn-area facility: in November 2026, the Virginia State Corporation Commission approved new Dominion Energy rates raising a typical residential bill by about $16 a month to roughly $165, while creating a new GS-5 data center rate class effective January 1, 2027, under which facilities with 25 megawatts or more of demand, a threshold this campus far exceeds, face 14-year mandatory contracts and minimum cost-coverage requirements, per Inside Climate News.

Northern Virginia's Loudoun and Prince William counties together form the largest data center market in the world by capacity, and local zoning debate has intensified as residents, county supervisors, and Dominion Energy weigh the tradeoff between substantial commercial tax revenue from facilities like this one and rising transmission-line construction, land consumption, and residential electricity-rate pressure tied to data center growth. Dominion Energy's long-range integrated resource plans have repeatedly cited this region's data center demand as the single largest driver of the utility's near-term generation and transmission capital spending, a dynamic that has drawn scrutiny from the Virginia State Corporation Commission in periodic rate cases. Vantage's Virginia cluster sits among the densest concentration of competing operators anywhere in the world, including Amazon Web Services, Equinix, Digital Realty, and QTS facilities within a few miles of this site.

profile.research_note: [process narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This Vantage Data Centers cluster is in Sterling, Virginia, part of the Northern Virginia Ashburn data center corridor. Vantage own site states the company began planning a 146 megawatt mega campus in Ashburn in October 2017, completing the first phase in February 2019 with 6 megawatts of IT capacity as an initial delivery. Vantage Data Centers was established in June 2010 with an investment from Silver Lake Partners, and Sureel Choksi became President and CEO in July 2013. DigitalBridge acquired Vantage in March 2017, and Silver Lake co-led a 9.2 billion dollar equity investment completed in June 2024. No building specific address or individual MW figures for this particular registry row were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
Vantage VA2 in Sterling publishes 96 MW of IT capacity, ranking third among Virginia facilities with disclosed megawatt figures and representing roughly 7 percent of the 1,326 MW total published across 19 sites in the state.

Ninety-six megawatts of IT load is substantial for AI workloads. Assuming 40 kW per rack, a common density for current AI training deployments, 96 MW supports roughly 2,400 racks. At 10 kW per rack, typical for general enterprise compute, the same power fills roughly 9,600 racks. These are assumptions about density, not operator claims. The published spec does not state rack count or supported density.

VA2 sits in the highest tier of disclosed capacity in Virginia, which is the densest concentration of data center infrastructure in the United States by mapped count. A 96 MW campus in that market is large enough to serve as a building block for hyperscale or large-model AI workloads, provided power delivery and network interconnection meet required specifications. Neither of those is confirmed by available data. The operator page does not publish certifications, tenant names, pricing, or connectivity details.
